title: Volume 11 · The First Ninety Days: Health Checks and Handing Over
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: the hypercare rhythm, the weekly health check, adoption evidence, and leaving without the client collapsing
outcomes: Run a hypercare rhythm that catches problems while they are still small
Perform a fifteen-minute weekly health check that a client can own
Measure adoption with evidence rather than anecdotes
Hand over to a successor so the client does not depend on any single person

slides.title: Hypercare is a rhythm, not a hotline
bullets: Week one has a fixed shape: a morning check, a same-day triage, and one written update per day
The first three days produce the real issue list, and the first weekend produces the real test
Nobody learns a new system and a new routine at once; keep the routine, change the system
Log every issue in one place from the first hour, even the ones solved by a phone call
The daily update is three lines: what broke, who owns it, what is at risk tomorrow
slides.notes: The rhythm is what stops hypercare becoming panic. A fixed morning check and one written update a day gives the client a heartbeat they can rely on, and gives you a record of what actually happened in the week that everyone later misremembers.

slides.title: Triage the fix list by consequence
bullets: Split the list into three: wrong numbers, blocked work, and cosmetic. Only the first two get fixed this month
A wrong number is a data or configuration defect and outranks everything, because trust in the ledger is the product
Blocked work is a training or permission problem more often than a missing feature
Cosmetic items go to one batch, agreed in advance, so the list has an end
Publish the triage decision, because a client who cannot see the reasoning assumes they were ignored

rows: Export the full issue list with owners
Mark each item wrong number, blocked or cosmetic
Fix wrong numbers first, with evidence
Resolve blocked work by training or permission
Publish the triage and the dates

slides.notes: The triage conversation is where trust is either built or lost. A cosmetic complaint fixed instantly while a wrong stock value waits teaches the client that volume wins. Publish the rule instead, then apply it to the loudest voice in the room.

slides.title: The first review, with numbers
bullets: Thirty days is long enough for real data and short enough to change course
Bring four numbers: open issues, wrong-number incidents, transaction volume and one adoption measure
Compare against the go-live baseline, not against an ideal, because the comparison is what means something
Agree three changes for the next month and write them down with owners
Invite the person who signs, not only the people who use the system

rows: For example delivery notes per order

slides.notes: The day-thirty review is where you find out whether the go-live was a success or merely a launch. Bring numbers, not narrative, and bring them compared to the baseline. Three actions with owners is the right size; ten is a wish list.

slides.title: The second-user test
bullets: By day sixty somebody other than the champion should be able to complete a core cycle unaided
Pick a cycle the business runs weekly: order to delivery, purchase to payment, count to reconciliation
Watch, do not help, and note every hesitation as a documentation or design defect
If only one person can do it, the project has built a dependency rather than a capability
Fix what you observe, then repeat the test with a third person

rows: Choose one weekly cycle and one second user
Ask them to run it while you watch
List of six to ten points
Fix the causes, not the symptoms
Record the result in the handover pack

slides.notes: The second-user test is the cheapest way to find out whether the training worked. Watching silently is the discipline: the moment you reach for the mouse you have learned nothing and taught dependence.

slides.title: Handing over to a successor, not an absence
bullets: The deliverable at ninety days is a named internal owner who can configure, not just operate
They should be able to add a user, a warehouse, a price list and a print format without calling you
Sit with them while they do it once, then sign them off in writing
Leave a support route with an agreed response time, so escalation is a decision rather than a habit
The test of the handover is a week where nothing is asked of you

rows: Name the internal owner and their deputy
Two names in the handover pack
Walk through adding a user with the right role
Add a warehouse and a price list together
Agree the support route and response time
Run one week with no questions to you

slides.notes: Handing over to a person rather than to a document is the difference between a project that ends and a project that never does. Name a deputy as well, because the owner takes leave, and the quiet week is the only real proof.

slides.title: Fifteen minutes that prevent most surprises
bullets: Five checks: overnight jobs ran, error log is quiet, stock and ledger reconcile, pending documents are not aging, backups completed
The scheduler failing silently is the most common cause of a surprise a month later
Aged drafts mean work that never became a transaction, and reports do not see it
Log the check with a date and a name, so a quiet week is provable later
Hand the check to the client's owner by week four, and watch them run it twice
slides.notes: Fifteen minutes a week is the cheapest maintenance in the whole engagement, and the one most often skipped once the consultant leaves. Hand it over with a printed sheet, and make the signature part of the routine rather than an audit afterthought.

slides.title: Prove use, do not assert it
bullets: Adoption is measurable: documents per week, users active, exceptions handled inside the system, print formats actually printed
A rising count of spreadsheets beside the system is the clearest sign of adoption failure
Look for workarounds: stock adjustments used as corrections, journals used as edits, one user posting for everyone
Interview two users per role and ask what they still do outside the system
Put the evidence in the ninety-day report with the baseline beside it

rows: Most of the role, not one person

slides.notes: Adoption numbers are easy to fake accidentally, because a single power user can produce impressive volume. Count active users per role, and look for the workarounds that tell you the system is being used around rather than used.

slides.title: A hundred pages nobody reads is not a handover
bullets: Four artefacts beat a manual: the weekly sheet, the four-page SOP, the change register and the continuity section
Write for the person who joins in a year, with today's names replaced by roles
Every procedure starts with the trigger, not the tool: when this happens, do that
Keep one index page that says where everything is, including what is not in the system
Test the knowledge by asking the owner to answer a question from it without you

rows: Owner answered a question from it

slides.notes: Volume is the enemy of a handover. Four artefacts that get used beat a manual that gets filed. The role-versus-name test is quick and revealing: if the procedure names a person who left, it is already historical.

slides.title: Three numbers after you go
bullets: Accuracy: stock count variance and ledger agreement, because everything else depends on it
Timeliness: how long a document takes from creation to submission, per cycle
Exceptions: cancellations, adjustments and manual journals per hundred transactions, which reveal process holes
A client watching three numbers will notice a change before it becomes a crisis
Agree who reads them and when, or they become a dashboard nobody opens
slides.notes: Three numbers, read monthly by a named person, is a working control. The exception rate is the most diagnostic and the least used: a rising count of manual journals usually means a process nobody documented is happening every week.

slides.title: Ending well is part of the deliverable
bullets: An exit is a dated moment with a signed handover, not a slow fade in response times
Close every open item explicitly: fixed, accepted, or transferred with a name against it
Return access you no longer need, and hand back the keys the client owns
Leave the successor's contact in writing, so the client knows who to call and why
Offer one optional review at quarter end, priced, so ongoing help is a choice rather than a dependency

rows: Close the open item list item by item
Sign the handover pack with the owner
Return or revoke your own access
Confirm the client holds every key and password
Write the successor and support route
Offer the quarter-end review in writing

slides.notes: The exit is judged by what the client can do the week after you leave, not by the closing meeting. Closing every item explicitly, returning access and naming the successor turns the end of a project into the start of a capability — which is the only outcome worth signing.

lab.title: Lab · Run a ninety-day close-out for Seri Murni
steps: Draw the hypercare rhythm on one page and run the morning check with a name and time against it
Triage a twenty-item fix list into wrong number, blocked and cosmetic, then publish three dates
Prepare the day-thirty review with four numbers compared against the go-live baseline
Run the second-user test on order to delivery and record every hesitation without helping
Perform the fifteen-minute weekly health check and sign the sheet
Collect adoption evidence per role and name the spreadsheets that have actually been retired
Sit with the internal owner while they add a user, a warehouse and a print format themselves
Complete the exit: close every open item, sign the handover, revoke your own access, offer one dated quarterly review
lab.done: A dated ninety-day close-out with a signed weekly health sheet, a published triage, an ownership test passed by a second user, adoption numbers per role, and an exit where the client holds every key and your access is closed.

quiz.question: What gives hypercare its structure in the first week?
options: A fixed morning check, same-day triage and one written update per day
quiz.why: A rhythm produces a heartbeat the client can rely on and a record of what happened. An open hotline produces neither, and memories of week one are always wrong.

quiz.question: In a fix-list triage, which category outranks the others?
options: Cosmetic complaints from the loudest user
Wrong numbers, because trust in the ledger is the product
quiz.why: A wrong number undermines every report built on it. Blocked work is usually training or permission; cosmetic items can be batched. A published rule stops volume deciding.

quiz.question: What does the second-user test actually prove?
options: That somebody other than the champion can complete a core cycle unaided
quiz.why: It measures capability rather than attendance. Watching without helping is what exposes the hesitations that documentation or design should have prevented.

quiz.question: Which weekly health check failure most often causes a surprise a month later?
options: A scheduler that stopped running without anyone noticing
quiz.why: Silent scheduler failures mean recurring documents and jobs simply stop, and nobody notices until a number is missing at month end.

quiz.question: What is the clearest evidence that adoption has failed despite busy transaction counts?
options: Spreadsheets proliferate beside the system to get the work done
quiz.why: Parallel spreadsheets mean the real work is happening outside, often done by one power user whose volume makes the dashboard look healthy.

memory.spine: Rhythm for the first week, triage by consequence, prove adoption with numbers, and leave a named owner who never needs you.

device.label: Week, month, quarter, exit
expansion: Week one: morning check, same-day triage, one written update a day
Month one: numbers at day thirty, three agreed actions with owners
Month two: a second user completes a weekly cycle unaided while you watch
Month three: the internal owner configures a user, a warehouse and a print format
Exit: every item closed, keys handed back, your access revoked, one dated offer

cards.q: What three things shape a hypercare week?
cards.a: A morning check with a name and time, same-day triage of anything wrong, and one written update per day. Everything else is optional.

cards.q: How should a fix list be split, and in what order?
cards.a: Wrong numbers first, then blocked work, then cosmetic in one agreed batch — and publish the rule so volume does not decide.

cards.q: Why is the second-user test more valuable than a training record?
cards.a: It measures capability: a non-champion completes a weekly cycle unaided while you watch in silence, exposing hesitations that training missed.

cards.q: Which five checks make up the weekly health routine?
cards.a: Scheduled jobs ran, error log quiet, stock and ledger agree, aged drafts counted, backups completed — signed with a date and a name.

cards.q: What does a good exit actually deliver?
cards.a: Every open item closed as fixed, accepted or transferred, keys handed back, your access revoked, a named successor, and one dated optional review.

trap.what: Hypercare drifts: response times lengthen quietly, the champion is the only user, and the consultant is still answering questions in month nine.
trap.why: Dependence feels like success and is the opposite. Set the exit date at the start, hand over to a named owner with a deputy, publish three numbers the client reads, and close every item explicitly when the date arrives.

narration: Go live is a launch, not an ending, and the ninety days after it decide whether the client owns a system or rents one. The first week needs a rhythm rather than a hotline: a morning check with a name and a time, same day triage of anything wrong, and one written update every day. Then triage the fix list by consequence. Wrong numbers first, because trust in the ledger is the product, then blocked work, which is usually training or a permission, then the cosmetic items in one agreed batch with a published rule so volume does not decide. At day thirty bring four numbers compared against the go-live baseline, and agree three actions with owners. At day sixty watch a second user, not the champion, complete a weekly cycle unaided, and record every hesitation as a defect rather than a training gap. At day ninety hand over to a named internal owner and a deputy, who can add a user, a warehouse and a print format without calling you. Along the way run the fifteen minute weekly check, prove adoption with counts per role instead of anecdotes, and finish with a dated exit: every item closed, keys handed back, your access revoked, and one optional review priced in writing.
